title: YU-LIN CHUNG
text:
I am currently pursuing a Master of Business in Data Analytics at Monash University.
I hold a bachelor’s degree in Language and Creative Writing from National Taipei University of Education and previously worked as a Social Marketing Specialist. My academic and professional background has led me to develop a strong interest in the intersection of creativity, communication, and data analysis.
In particular, I am interested in how analytical methods and algorithms can be used to better understand creative content and audience behaviour, and how these insights can support more effective and evidence-based approaches to social media marketing.

title: Did Climate Change Make Australia’s Black Summer More Likely?
text:
Australia’s 2019–20 Black Summer was one of the country’s worst bushfire seasons. Extreme heat, dry conditions and dangerous fire weather came together across southeastern Australia, while smoke blanketed cities, harmed public health and placed extra pressure on health services. Understanding why these conditions became so extreme matters because the consequences reached far beyond the fires themselves.
So the obvious question is:
Did climate change make the Black Summer more likely?
The answer is yes. Using long-term temperature and rainfall observations, ERA5 weather data and 11 large climate-model ensembles, a 2021 study by van Oldenborgh et al. examined how human-caused climate change affected extreme heat, drought and fire-weather conditions during the Black Summer. The clearest evidence appeared in extreme heat and severe fire weather. (Oldenborgh et al. 2021)

title: Did Climate Change Make Australia’s Black Summer More Likely?
section: How did climate change change the weather behind the fires?
text:
How did climate change change the weather behind the fires?
The clearest climate-change signal appeared in extreme heat and fire weather.
The bigger problem of the Black Summer was that several weather conditions came together to create an environment in which fires could become much harder to control. One way scientists describe this is through fire weather — the combination of heat, rainfall, humidity and wind that affects how easily a fire can spread and how difficult it may be to suppress. (Oldenborgh et al. 2021)












What was studied
How it was measured




Extreme heat
The hottest 7-day period


Drought
Annual rainfall and the driest month of the fire season


Fire weather
An index combining temperature, rainfall, humidity and wind






Table 1: How the study measured the weather behind the Black Summer. Source: van Oldenborgh et al. (2021).




To understand the results, it helps to first see how the study separated the weather conditions behind the Black Summer. Table 1 gives a quick overview of the three parts of the analysis.
A week as hot as the one experienced in December 2019 was at least twice as likely because of human-caused warming. A comparable heatwave in the early twentieth century would also have been around 1–2°C cooler.
Fire weather showed a similar pattern. Climate models estimated that conditions as severe as those seen in 2019–20 had become about 80% more likely. Because the models tended to underestimate the observed rise in extreme heat and fire weather, the authors reported a more cautious conclusion: at least 30% more likely.
The risk is also expected to keep rising. At 2°C of global warming, similar extreme fire-weather conditions could become at least four times as likely as they were in the early twentieth century.
As shown in Figure 1, the likelihood of extreme fire-weather conditions rises sharply as the climate warms.








Figure 1: Relative likelihood of extreme fire-weather conditions under different levels of global warming. Values show conservative lower-bound estimates relative to the early twentieth-century climate, based on van Oldenborgh et al. (2021).

title: Did Climate Change Make Australia’s Black Summer More Likely?
section: The drought result was less clear
text:
The drought result was less clear
For the rainfall measures used in the analysis, there was no clear evidence that climate change had made the 2019 drought more likely.
That does not mean climate change had no effect on the Black Summer. It means the drought signal was harder to separate from natural climate variability. Additionally, Natural patterns such as the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Southern Annular Mode (SAM) also contributed to the unusually dry conditions in 2019.

title: Did Climate Change Make Australia’s Black Summer More Likely?
section: So, did climate change make the Black Summer more likely?
text:
So, did climate change make the Black Summer more likely?
Yes. Human-caused climate change made the extreme heat and dangerous fire weather behind the Black Summer more likely, although the drought signal was much less clear. But the importance of this result goes beyond one fire season. At 2°C of global warming, similar extreme fire-weather conditions will happen in the future. (Oldenborgh et al. 2021)
The Black Summer showed how quickly existing systems can be pushed to their limits. That means future bushfire planning cannot rely only on what Australia has experienced in the past. Understanding how climate change is shifting fire-weather risk can help inform risk assessments, emergency preparedness, evacuation planning and land-use decisions. The challenge now is to use that knowledge to prepare for a climate in which these conditions may no longer be so unusual.
